transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Well, I came in because I... I just can’t seem to stop launching projects. Work plans, new certification schedules... I actually just bought this massive glass whiteboard for my home office to track it all. It’s one of those frosted glass ones, you know? They look so much sleeker than the standard cheap ones that stain if you leave the dry-erase marker on too long. I really hate when that happens, especially with the red markers. Red is impossible to get off. 

But anyway, I'm just constantly mapping out home network upgrades and sending out messages to old contacts. I even reached out to this guy Dave from my undergrad—we did our capstone project together on database architecture, and he actually lives in Denver now. Great skiing out there, apparently. I've never been, but I went down a whole rabbit hole watching videos about it the other night. 

Wait, what was I saying? Right, the projects. It just gets so intense that I completely blow past normal limits. I just keep going and going until my wife or my director at work literally has to step in and shut me down.
Have you had any hallucinations, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others could not?

Um, yeah, I guess I do. Sometimes when I'm at work, or even just sitting in my home office when my wife isn't around and it's completely empty... I'll hear my name. Or these short little comments, like "check the logs" or "they know." It always seems to come right out of the hum of the servers, or the computer fans. 

Have you ever been in a real data center? The hum is incredibly intense. It's mostly the cooling systems, the CRAC units—that stands for Computer Room Air Conditioning. We actually had to replace two of ours last quarter because they were leaking condensation near the racks, which is obviously a massive hazard. Getting the budget approved for that was a total nightmare, though. Finance always pushes back on infrastructure spending because they don't see the immediate ROI. I had this whole back-and-forth with Linda, our CFO, about it. She just doesn't get that if the servers fry, the entire company goes dark. She's so obsessed with quarterly margins, which I mean, I get it, her background is in corporate accounting, but you can't cut corners on thermal management... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, hearing things. Yeah, so it's just those quick comments in the background noise, mostly.
Have you been able to sleep much less than usual without feeling tired?

Yeah, definitely. There have been these runs lately where I sleep maybe... three hours? I'll wake up sharp at 3 or 4 a.m., and instead of feeling exhausted, I feel like I've just been handed this incredible gift of bonus time. It's actually the best time to work, honestly, because no one is emailing you. 

I use this app to track my sleep cycles, actually. It uses the accelerometer in my smartwatch to monitor my movement during the night. The technology is pretty fascinating—it graphs out your REM sleep versus deep sleep. I was looking into the API for it the other day because I wanted to export the raw data into a custom dashboard I'm building. I figured if I could correlate my sleep metrics with the server load times during my late-night coding sessions, I might find some interesting patterns. Data visualization is getting so advanced now. Have you seen what they can do with Python libraries like Seaborn? It's incredible. You can create these beautiful heat maps... 

Um, anyway, yeah. Three hours of sleep and I'm totally wired, ready to go.
Do you believe the voices you hear are real, or do you recognize that they may be coming from your mind?

Um... well, it's hard to say. I mean, in the moment, when I hear "check the logs," it sounds totally real. It's just right there in the air. But then I think about it logically, and I know servers don't talk. 

Speaking of servers, we just migrated to a new cloud-based infrastructure last month. It was supposed to be a seamless transition, but of course, it wasn't. The vendor promised zero downtime, which is always a red flag. I mean, anyone who guarantees 100% uptime is either lying or doesn't understand the physical limitations of hardware. We ended up having this massive latency issue because the data centers were routing through a node in Virginia instead of the local one here. I spent like three days straight on the phone with their Tier 3 support team. The guy I was talking to, Marcus, was actually really sharp. He used to work for the NSA, apparently. Or at least a contractor for them. The security protocols they use over there are insane. They have these air-gapped systems where... 

Wait, sorry. I lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, the voices. Yeah, I don't know. Sometimes I think they're real, sometimes I think it's just my brain playing tricks on me.
Have you ever had a period where your mood was so elevated or irritable that it caused major problems or you needed hospitalization?

Yeah, I mean... some weeks I feel almost electric. Just totally unstoppable, like my brain is processing at a higher clock speed and I can just get everything done at once. 

Actually, speaking of electricity, we had to do a massive overhaul of the UPS—the uninterruptible power supplies—at the office last year. The battery backups we had were just ancient. Lead-acid batteries degrade so fast if you don't maintain them properly, and the previous IT manager just let them sit there for years. If we'd had a brownout, the whole network would have dropped instantly. I had to source these new lithium-ion racks, which are way lighter and have a much better lifecycle, but the supply chain issues were ridiculous. I was tracking shipments from Taiwan every single morning. Shipping logistics are a complete nightmare right now, honestly. They use these massive container ships that burn bunker fuel, which is obviously terrible for the environment, but it's really the only way to move that kind of tonnage across the Pacific. The routing algorithms they use to manage the ports are pretty fascinating, though... 

Wait, sorry. What were you asking? Oh, right, my mood causing problems. Yeah, so when I'm having one of those weeks where I feel unstoppable, the flip side is that I get incredibly frustrated if anything gets in my way. Like, if there's even a tiny delay with a project, or if my wife just asks me a simple question while I'm working, I can completely snap at her. It just feels like everyone is trying to slow me down on purpose, you know? Like they're intentionally dragging their feet just to mess up my momentum.
Have you ever been hospitalized because of one of these high-energy or irritable episodes?

No, I haven't been hospitalized. But it definitely caused some major issues. After that whole server migration thing failed, work actually put me on administrative leave. They said I needed to "take a step back," which I still think was a massive overreaction. 

Speaking of stepping back, I used to do a lot of indoor rock climbing. Have you ever tried bouldering? It's completely different from top-rope climbing. It's all about problem-solving. You look at the wall, and they call the routes "problems," and you have to figure out the exact sequence of moves—the beta—to get to the top. The chalk they use is magnesium carbonate, and it's crazy how much friction it adds. I was actually looking into the chemical properties of different chalk brands because some of them use drying agents that completely wreck your skin. You have to use this special salve made from beeswax...

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, the leave from work. Yeah, so I've been home, and my wife has basically had to take over everything. She's been monitoring our bank accounts because of my spending, and she literally unplugs the router sometimes to stop my late-night work sessions. We end up arguing a lot because she tries to talk to me and I just... snap. I've also completely pulled away from playing music at church, and I stopped mentoring the junior devs. I just can't seem to show up reliably or follow through on anything right now.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you felt very down or lost interest or pleasure in things?

Yeah... yeah, definitely. There are these stretches, usually lasting a few weeks or more, where I just wake up feeling like this completely failed version of myself. Everything feels so heavy and flat, you know? Even just answering my wife's normal, everyday questions feels like it takes this massive amount of effort, like it's just too much to handle. 

Which is weird, because usually I'm so quick to process information. Like, when I was optimizing the SQL queries for our backend database, I could spot the bottlenecks instantly. A lot of developers don't realize that using a SELECT * statement is incredibly inefficient if you only need a few columns. It pulls all this unnecessary data into the buffer pool, which just crushes your memory. I had to write this massive documentation on indexing strategies for the team. Did you know that a B-tree index is basically useless if you're querying a column with low cardinality? Like a boolean field. The query optimizer will just do a full table scan anyway because it's faster than traversing the tree. It's fascinating how the engine makes those decisions under the hood...

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, feeling down. Yeah, so when I get like that, I just don't care about any of it. The databases, the music, everything just feels pointless and I can't even get out of bed sometimes.
Have you ever had a time when you were hearing voices or believing things like that even though your mood was not unusually high, irritable, or depressed?

Yeah, actually. There have been these... calm stretches, I guess you'd call them. Like, a few weeks at a time where my mood isn't really up or down. I'm not depressed, I'm not feeling that electric high, just kind of flat. But even then, I still notice things. Like the Microsoft Teams statuses at work. I know they're coded warnings. People think it's just "Available" or "Busy," but the timing of when they switch, it's a very specific sequence. 

Which, honestly, Teams is such a resource hog. The Electron framework it's built on is notorious for memory leaks. You can just watch your RAM usage spike in the Task Manager when you have it open. It's because every Electron app is basically running its own instance of Chromium in the background. It's incredibly lazy development. If they just wrote native apps for each OS, it would run so much smoother, but everyone wants a unified codebase now. I actually started writing a lightweight wrapper for the Teams API just to avoid using the desktop client, but Microsoft's documentation on their Graph API is a complete mess. They deprecate endpoints without warning...

Sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, hearing things when my mood is normal. Yeah, even during those flat weeks, I still hear these brief comments. Just... voices, when no one is in the room. And I still see the patterns in the Teams statuses. So it doesn't really stop, even when my mood is fine.
Have there ever been at least two weeks when you were hearing or seeing things even though your mood was not high, low, or irritable?

Yeah, like I was just saying... there have been several of those calm, flat stretches. Usually a few weeks at a time where I'm not depressed, and I'm definitely not feeling that high or irritable energy. Just... normal mood, I guess. But even during those weeks, I still believed the Teams statuses were those coded warnings I mentioned. And I still heard those brief comments when no one was around. 

It's actually really frustrating when things don't work the way they're supposed to. Like our smart home setup. I spent three whole weekends wiring the entire house with Cat6 cable so we wouldn't have to rely on Wi-Fi for the main devices. Wi-Fi is so susceptible to interference, especially if you live in a dense neighborhood. Everyone's router is blasting on the 2.4 gigahertz band, and the channels just overlap and cause packet loss. It's a nightmare for latency. I set up a dedicated pfSense router on an old Dell Optiplex I bought off eBay, and the granular control you get over the firewall rules is incredible. You can actually route specific VLANs through a VPN tunnel at the hardware level...

Wait, sorry. Did I already answer your question? I think I did. Yeah, the weeks with normal mood but still having the warnings and the voices. That definitely happens for at least two weeks at a time.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you had hallucinations or fixed strange beliefs while your mood was completely normal?

Yeah, I mean, I feel like we just covered this, but yes. There have been several of those calm, flat stretches. Like a few weeks at a time where I wasn't feeling especially up, and I wasn't depressed either. Just completely normal. But I still believed the Teams statuses were those coded warnings, and I still heard those brief comments when no one was there. 

It's kind of like when you think a system is stable, but there's a background process just eating up CPU cycles. I was actually monitoring my home server the other day, and I noticed this weird spike in I/O operations. I run a RAID 5 array for redundancy, because I've had hard drives fail on me before and losing data is just not an option. But RAID 5 has that write penalty because it has to calculate the parity bits across all the drives. It's fine for sequential reads, but if you're doing a lot of random small writes, the performance just tanks. I probably should have gone with RAID 10, but you lose half your raw storage capacity, and I have a massive Plex library. I've got terabytes of high-bitrate 4K rips, and... 

Sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? But yeah, to answer your question, yes. At least two weeks of normal mood while still having the warnings and the voices.
Have you ever had any hallucinations or fixed strange beliefs when you were having a high or irritable mood, or were those symptoms only present when your mood was normal?

Yeah, they definitely happen then, too. During those really driven stretches—you know, when I'm barely sleeping, just wired and pushing huge plans forward—I still get them. Like, I'd be hearing these comments mixed in with the server noise, or reading hidden threats into regular work messages. 

Which is actually why I prefer mechanical keyboards when I'm working like that. The tactile feedback is just so much better. I use Cherry MX Brown switches because the Blues are just too loud, especially if you're on a call. But the Browns give you that nice little bump without the click. I actually built my own custom 60% board a while back. Sourced the PCB, hand-lubed all the stabilizers because otherwise you get this awful rattling sound on the spacebar... It took hours, but it's totally worth it. The stock boards you buy from Corsair or Razer, they just use cheap ABS keycaps that get all shiny after a few months of typing. PBT plastic is way more durable, it keeps that nice matte texture... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, when I'm in that high gear, not sleeping, I still hear the comments and see the threats. It's not just when my mood is flat.
Have there ever been at least two weeks when you were having the voices or strange beliefs while you were not having any mood symptoms at all—no elevated, irritable, or depressed mood?

Yeah, I mean... I feel like we're kind of going in circles here, but yes. I definitely have those calm stretches. Like, there have been times, maybe a few weeks at a stretch, where I'm not up, I'm not depressed, I'm not irritable. Just flat. No mood stuff at all. But even then, I still believed the Teams statuses were those coded warnings, and I still heard those brief comments when no one was around. 

It's actually a lot like troubleshooting a network issue when the physical layer seems completely fine. You check the cables, you use a fluke tester, everything passes. But you're still dropping packets. I had this issue with a switch in my rack last month. It was a managed gigabit switch, and the web interface was showing zero errors on the ports. But every time I tried to transfer large files over the local network, the throughput would just plummet. I thought maybe it was a bad crimp on the RJ45 connectors, so I re-terminated like ten different cables. You have to get the wire order exactly right—orange-white, orange, green-white, blue, blue-white, green, brown-white, brown. If you mess up the twist rate near the connector, you get crosstalk. Anyway, I spent hours on it, and it turned out to be a firmware bug in the switch itself. I had to flash it via a serial console cable...

Sorry, I'm rambling again. But yes, to your question—two weeks of no mood symptoms at all, but still having the warnings and the voices. Yes, that definitely happens.
During your high-energy periods, have you ever become so impaired that you needed to be hospitalized or couldn't take care of yourself?

Well, I haven't been hospitalized, no. But impaired... yeah, I guess things get pretty out of hand. Like, I actually got put on leave at work recently after this huge migration project completely fell apart. I was just pushing too hard, changing configurations on the fly, not sleeping... 

Which reminds me, sleep is just so critical for cognitive function, you know? I read this study about how cerebrospinal fluid actually washes through the brain during deep sleep to clear out amyloid beta proteins. It's like a garbage collection process in a programming language. If you don't run the garbage collector, you get memory leaks, and eventually the whole application crashes. I used to write a lot of C++ back in college, and manual memory management is such a nightmare. You have to explicitly allocate and deallocate memory using pointers. If you forget to delete an object, it just sits there taking up RAM. That's why languages like Python and Java are so much more popular now for general development, because they handle all that in the background. Though, to be fair, you take a performance hit with garbage collection. If you're writing high-frequency trading algorithms or game engines, you still need that bare-metal control...

Right, sorry, the impairment. Yeah, so work put me on leave. And at home, it's been rough. My wife has had to step in a lot. Like, I'll start spending way too much on server parts, or working until 4 AM, and when she tries to talk to me about it, it just turns into this massive argument. I've also completely dropped out of my usual stuff. I used to play music at church, go rock climbing, mentor some junior devs... but I just can't reliably show up or follow through on anything right now. So yeah, I'd say it gets pretty bad.
When you are not having any mood symptoms and those voices or strange beliefs are still there, do they ever make it hard for you to work, care for yourself, or get through the day?

No, not really. When my mood is flat and it's just the voices or the, you know, the warnings... I can usually function okay. It doesn't stop me from getting through the day or doing my job. I mean, my job is mostly remote anyway, which helps. 

Actually, working remotely has completely changed how I set up my home office. I invested in this Herman Miller Aeron chair, and it's incredible. The ergonomics on it are just next level. It has this Pellicle suspension material instead of foam, so it distributes your weight evenly and doesn't trap heat. It's so much better than those racing-style gaming chairs. Those things are terrible for your lumbar spine. They just push your shoulders forward and give you zero lower back support. I read this whole breakdown on how the bucket seat design was originally made to keep race car drivers from sliding around during high-G turns, which makes absolutely no sense for someone sitting at a desk typing. But they market them to gamers, and people just buy them up because they look cool on Twitch streams...

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the flat mood stuff. Yeah, when it's just that, I'm fine. I can still work and take care of things. It doesn't really get in the way.
Over the entire time you’ve been ill, have mood episodes like your high-energy or depressed periods been present for most of the illness, or only for a smaller part of it?

Well, looking back... yeah, the high-energy, pressured phases have definitely taken up more of these past couple years than the down periods or the quieter in-between times. It feels like I'm almost always running hot, you know? 

Which, honestly, kind of reminds me of how my main server rack was running before I upgraded the cooling system. I was using these standard 120-millimeter case fans, and they just weren't pulling enough CFM—cubic feet per minute—to keep the ambient temperature down. The CPUs were thermal throttling constantly. Thermal throttling is when the processor intentionally slows down its clock speed to prevent physical damage from overheating. It's a built-in safety mechanism, but it completely tanks your performance. I had to rip out all the old fans and install these high-static-pressure Noctua fans. They're kind of ugly—they have this weird brown and beige color scheme that clashes with literally everything—but the acoustic profile is amazing. They use this special bearing design that makes them practically silent even at high RPMs. I also applied some new thermal paste to the CPU coolers. You have to be really careful not to put too much on, just a pea-sized drop in the center, or it squishes out over the edges of the heat spreader and makes a huge mess. Plus, if it's conductive paste, you can short out the motherboard...

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the mood stuff. Yeah, the high-energy, running-hot periods have definitely been the majority of the time I've been dealing with all this.
Have you ever had a period where your mood was so high or irritable that you became completely unable to function normally, like needing hospitalization or being severely out of control?

Well, I haven't been hospitalized, like I mentioned, but out of control? Yeah, I guess so. Some weeks I feel almost electric, you know? Like I'm just completely unstoppable. But then, if there's even a tiny delay, or if my wife just asks a simple question, I can just snap. It feels like everyone is intentionally trying to slow me down on purpose. 

It's actually a lot like network latency. When you have high latency, every single packet of data takes longer to reach its destination, and it causes this infuriating lag. I was troubleshooting this network bottleneck last month, and it turned out to be a faulty switch that was dropping packets. Packet loss is the absolute worst because the TCP protocol has to constantly retransmit the lost data, which just creates this massive traffic jam on the network. It's why UDP is better for streaming video or VoIP calls—it just fires the packets and doesn't care if they all arrive in perfect order. But for file transfers, you absolutely need TCP to guarantee data integrity. I ended up swapping out the switch for a managed Cisco one, which let me configure VLANs to segment the traffic and prioritize the critical stuff. VLANs are great because they act like separate physical networks even though they're running on the same hardware, which really helps with security and broadcast storms...

Sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? But yeah, when I'm feeling that electric, unstoppable way, I get really irritable if anyone gets in my way or slows me down.
Have you ever had a period where you felt so unusually high or irritable that you became completely unable to function normally?

Well, yeah, I guess so. I mean, things definitely got out of control at work. I was actually put on leave after this big server migration completely failed. Which, to be fair, was a disaster from the start because the legacy system was running on an outdated SQL database, and trying to map those old tables to the new schema was just a nightmare. You have to be so careful with data normalization or you end up with all these redundant entries that bloat the database and slow down query times. I tried writing a custom script in Python to automate the data extraction, but the API rate limits kept throttling my requests. APIs can be so finicky, especially when they use OAuth 2.0 for authentication and the access tokens keep expiring right in the middle of a batch job... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the leave. Yeah, they put me on leave. And at home, it's been... well, my wife has really had to step in. She's been managing the spending because I was buying all this new hardware, and she tries to stop me from working all night. And we argue a lot—like, conversations just turn into these huge fights. I've also kind of dropped out of everything else. I used to do church music, go rock climbing, and I was mentoring this junior developer, but I just... I pulled away from all of it because I can't reliably show up or actually follow through on anything right now.
Have there ever been any hallucinations or strange beliefs for at least two weeks when your mood was normal and you were not having a manic or depressive episode?

Yeah, looking back, there have definitely been these calm stretches. Like, a few weeks at a time where I wasn't running hot, and I wasn't feeling depressed either. Just kind of flat and normal. But even during those weeks, I still completely believed that the Microsoft Teams statuses at work were coded warnings specifically for me. And I'd still hear those brief comments in the room when no one else was there. 

Speaking of Teams, the way it handles those presence statuses—the little green, yellow, or red dots—is actually a huge drain on system resources. It constantly polls the Microsoft Graph API to update the state across the tenant. And because the classic client was built on the Electron framework, it basically runs a full instance of the Chromium browser in the background just to render the UI. It's a massive memory hog. I've seen it eat up like two gigabytes of RAM just sitting idle on a user's machine. Microsoft finally started rolling out the new client that uses Edge WebView2 instead, which is supposed to cut memory usage in half, but the transition has been a total headache for our deployment endpoints. You have to push out the new MSIX package via Intune, but half the time the old client doesn't uninstall cleanly, leaving these orphaned registry keys that completely mess up the file associations and Outlook integrations...

But um, sorry, I'm getting off track again. Yeah. Even when my mood is completely stable for a few weeks, I still get those coded warnings from the statuses and hear the comments.

When you have these voices or coded messages, do they ever include themes that are clearly about your mood episodes—for example, when you're depressed do they say you’re worthless, or when you’re high do they seem especially grand or upbeat?

Well, no, not exactly. The messages and the voices... they don't really change their tune based on how I'm feeling. Like, they don't tell me I'm worthless when I'm down or anything like that. But they definitely happen at the same time as the mood stuff. Like, during my most driven stretches, when I was barely sleeping and pushing these huge plans for the network overhaul, I was also hearing comments in the server noise and reading hidden threats into work messages. 

Which, by the way, server noise is no joke. If you've ever stood in a hot aisle of a data center, the decibel level from the cooling fans alone can cause permanent hearing damage if you aren't wearing ear protection. Those 1U rack servers have these tiny, high-RPM fans that just scream when the CPU load spikes. We had this one chassis where the thermal paste on the heat sinks had dried out, so the processors were constantly thermal throttling. The fans were running at 100% duty cycle, 24/7. I ended up having to schedule a maintenance window at 2 AM on a Sunday just to pull the blades out, clean off the old crusty paste with isopropyl alcohol, and reapply it. You have to use a good quality paste, like Arctic Silver, or you're just going to be doing it all over again in six months. And applying it is an art—you don't want to use too much or it spills over the edges of the die, but too little and you get air pockets...

Anyway, what was I... right. The voices and the messages. Yeah, they were happening right in the middle of all that high-energy, no-sleep time, but they weren't, like, cheering me on or anything. Just the same weird comments and threats.
Have there been any times when the voices or strange beliefs were present only during your manic or depressed episodes and completely went away when your mood was normal?

Well, no, actually. I think I mentioned this just a minute ago, but yeah, there have definitely been stretches where my mood was totally normal—just kind of flat, not up, not down—and the voices and beliefs didn't go away at all. Like I said, I'd have a few weeks at a time where I felt fine, but I still completely believed the Teams statuses were those coded warnings, and I was still hearing those brief comments in empty rooms. 

Which is really frustrating, because you'd think if your mood levels out, the rest of the system would stabilize too. It's kind of like when you have a memory leak in an application. You can restart the service, and everything looks fine on the performance monitor for a while, CPU usage drops, disk I/O goes back to baseline... but the underlying code is still holding onto those memory allocations. So even though the system seems stable, the application is still broken, and eventually, the worker process is going to crash again. We had this issue with a custom middleware app that was supposed to bridge our HR software with Active Directory. The developer didn't properly dispose of the LDAP connection objects, so every time someone's title changed, it just spawned a new connection and left the old one hanging. I had to go into the source code myself and wrap the whole block in a 'using' statement so the garbage collector would actually clean it up... 

But yeah, sorry. To answer your question, no, they don't go away when my mood is normal. I still get the warnings and hear the comments even during those calm stretches.

doctor.intent: Open the interview and elicit the main presenting problem so I can narrow the differential diagnosis.
doctor.question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can’t seem to stop launching projects—work plans, certification schedules, home network upgrades, messages to old contacts—and it gets so intense that I blow past normal limits until my wife or my director has to step in.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return my chief complaint.

patient.answer:
Hi, doctor. Well, I came in because I... I just can’t seem to stop launching projects. Work plans, new certification schedules... I actually just bought this massive glass whiteboard for my home office to track it all. It’s one of those frosted glass ones, you know? They look so much sleeker than the standard cheap ones that stain if you leave the dry-erase marker on too long. I really hate when that happens, especially with the red markers. Red is impossible to get off. 

But anyway, I'm just constantly mapping out home network upgrades and sending out messages to old contacts. I even reached out to this guy Dave from my undergrad—we did our capstone project together on database architecture, and he actually lives in Denver now. Great skiing out there, apparently. I've never been, but I went down a whole rabbit hole watching videos about it the other night.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during mood episodes or also persist independently, which separates schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features and schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Have there ever been any hallucinations or strange beliefs for at least two weeks when your mood was normal and you were not having a manic or depressive episode?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There have been several calm or flat stretches, including a few weeks at a time, when I wasn’t especially up or depressed but still believed Teams statuses were coded warnings and still heard brief comments when no one was there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have experienced hallucinations or strange beliefs for at least two weeks when my mood was normal, which matches the criteria for psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah, looking back, there have definitely been these calm stretches. Like, a few weeks at a time where I wasn't running hot, and I wasn't feeling depressed either. Just kind of flat and normal. But even during those weeks, I still completely believed that the Microsoft Teams statuses at work were coded warnings specifically for me. And I'd still hear those brief comments in the room when no one else was there. 

Speaking of Teams, the way it handles those presence statuses—the little green, yellow, or red dots—is actually a huge drain on system resources. It constantly polls the Microsoft Graph API to update the state across the tenant. And because the classic client was built on the Electron framework, it basically runs a full instance of the Chromium browser in the background just to render the UI. It's a massive memory hog. I've seen it eat up like two gigabytes of RAM just sitting idle on a user's machine. Microsoft finally started rolling out the new client that uses Edge WebView2 instead, which is supposed to cut memory usage in half, but the transition has been a total headache for our deployment endpoints. You have to push out the new MSIX package via Intune, but half the time the old client doesn't uninstall cleanly, leaving these orphaned registry keys that completely mess up the file associations and Outlook integrations...

But um, sorry, I'm getting off track again. Yeah. Even when my mood is completely stable for a few weeks, I still get those coded warnings from the statuses and hear the comments.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are mood-incongruent, which helps distinguish schizoaffective disorder subtypes from bipolar disorder with psychotic features
doctor.question: When you have these voices or coded messages, do they ever include themes that are clearly about your mood episodes—for example, when you're depressed do they say you’re worthless, or when you’re high do they seem especially grand or upbeat?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: During my most driven stretches, when I was barely sleeping and pushing huge plans, I was also hearing comments in the server noise and reading hidden threats into work messages.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the themes of the psychotic symptoms during mood episodes (e.g., whether they are grandiose when high). This item describes the specific nature of the psychotic symptoms (hearing comments and reading hidden threats) during the manic, driven stretches, addressing the question about their content during those episodes.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not exactly. The messages and the voices... they don't really change their tune based on how I'm feeling. Like, they don't tell me I'm worthless when I'm down or anything like that. But they definitely happen at the same time as the mood stuff. Like, during my most driven stretches, when I was barely sleeping and pushing these huge plans for the network overhaul, I was also hearing comments in the server noise and reading hidden threats into work messages. 

Which, by the way, server noise is no joke. If you've ever stood in a hot aisle of a data center, the decibel level from the cooling fans alone can cause permanent hearing damage if you aren't wearing ear protection. Those 1U rack servers have these tiny, high-RPM fans that just scream when the CPU load spikes. We had this one chassis where the thermal paste on the heat sinks had dried out, so the processors were constantly thermal throttling. The fans were running at 100% duty cycle, 24/7. I ended up having to schedule a maintenance window at 2 AM on a Sunday just to pull the blades out, clean off the old crusty paste with isopropyl alcohol, and reapply it. You have to use a good quality paste, like Arctic Silver, or you're just going to be doing it all over again in six months. And applying it is an art—you don't want to use too much or it spills over the edges of the die, but too little and you get air pockets...

Anyway, what was I... right. The voices and the messages. Yeah, they were happening right in the middle of all that high-energy, no-sleep time, but they weren't, like, cheering me on or anything. Just the same weird comments and threats.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had a period of psychosis occurring exclusively during mood episodes, which would distinguish schizoaffective bipolar type from schizophrenia with mood symptoms and help clarify current episode severity.
doctor.question: Have there been any times when the voices or strange beliefs were present only during your manic or depressed episodes and completely went away when your mood was normal?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There have been several calm or flat stretches, including a few weeks at a time, when I wasn’t especially up or depressed but still believed Teams statuses were coded warnings and still heard brief comments when no one was there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the psychotic symptoms only occur during mood episodes, which directly relates to the criterion of whether they occur in the absence of a mood episode.

patient.answer:
Well, no, actually. I think I mentioned this just a minute ago, but yeah, there have definitely been stretches where my mood was totally normal—just kind of flat, not up, not down—and the voices and beliefs didn't go away at all. Like I said, I'd have a few weeks at a time where I felt fine, but I still completely believed the Teams statuses were those coded warnings, and I was still hearing those brief comments in empty rooms. 

Which is really frustrating, because you'd think if your mood levels out, the rest of the system would stabilize too. It's kind of like when you have a memory leak in an application. You can restart the service, and everything looks fine on the performance monitor for a while, CPU usage drops, disk I/O goes back to baseline... but the underlying code is still holding onto those memory allocations. So even though the system seems stable, the application is still broken, and eventually, the worker process is going to crash again. We had this issue with a custom middleware app that was supposed to bridge our HR software with Active Directory. The developer didn't properly dispose of the LDAP connection objects, so every time someone's title changed, it just spawned a new connection and left the old one hanging. I had to go into the source code myself and wrap the whole block in a 'using' statement so the garbage collector would actually clean it up... 

But yeah, sorry. To answer your question, no, they don't go away when my mood is normal. I still get the warnings and hear the comments even during those calm stretches.

opening_question.intent: Open the interview and elicit the main presenting problem so I can narrow the differential diagnosis.
opening_question.question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview confirms schizophrenia-like psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations, bizarre/paranoid delusional beliefs, ideas of reference) occurring for at least 2 weeks in the absence of mood symptoms, while also showing substantial mood episodes (manic/hypomanic-like high-energy periods and major depressive periods) that occupy a large part of the illness. This pattern is most consistent with schizoaffective disorder, manic type, rather than bipolar disorder with psychotic features or schizoaffective depressive type.
